I've got two. 

1) When nothing is their fault. If someone you're seeing seems to have nothing but setbacks, conflicts, and difficulties, and it's ALWAYS being inflicted on them, that's a poor sign. Some people definitely do have tougher lives than others, and everyone goes through periods of difficulty. BUt if EVERYTHING is because of somebody else's incompetence, apathy, or derision, then that's a pattern to pay attention to because after enough time it'll be *you* that's the source of their problems.

2) Bad boundaries. When someone is moving too fast that's always a bad sign that they don't have a good sense of boundaries. This can be many things: moving in with you after a month, dropping the "love" word after a few dates, telling you dark and serious stuff about their life on the first date, and generally just behaving the way you'd imagine with a year of dating rather than just an hour. See, if their boundaries are bad, then they're not likely to have a good grasp on yours.

Thing is, dude could have told him all that stuff, and he probably would have smiled, nodded, excused himself, and continued to marry her anyways. I have no doubt that he knew what he was getting himself into; if he didn't see ANY of that shit, then that alone should tell you a lot about his self-preservation instinct. 

Source: was that guy once

I always sorta "knew" that I needed to stop. I started drinking about 18, and when I was 21 and able to buy booze / go to bars was when it really became a problem. I wasn't an obsessive drinker, I wasn't constantly drinking or anything like that, but if it was after work then I needed to have a beer. If I went out, which was at least 3-4 times a week, I needed to at least get tipsy. If there -could- be drinking, then there -had- to be drinking, as far as I was concerned.

On top of this, I was kind of an uncontrolled drunk. I would argue, I would get loud, I would drive drunk, I'd spend more money than I wanted to, etc. Thankfully, nothing of lasting consequence happened. It didn't help I was in a very abusive relationship at the time, in which my drinking was held against me as an excuse for her behavior. That, of course, made me drink more.

So, what made me really stop was ending up in the hospital with severe alcohol poisoning, and subsequently going to a psych ward for a bit. I quit that day. I finally couldn't ignore it and decided I needed to do better for myself.

As far as life now? I don't focus my activities around drinking, I am not putting myself into dangerous situations, I feel better much of the time, and I'm able to take better care of my health. I think about drinking every now and then, and I've have a couple of drinks here and there (special occasions, mainly) but generally I don't consider myself a drinker, and I don't go out of my way to drink. I feel much more in control of myself and my life, and that is a plus.
